title: Automating inventory alerts without losing the relationship
metaTitle: Inventory alerts that stay inside the team
excerpt: Alert the person who reorders when stock crosses a line they chose. Do not email customers a restock date or a fake scarcity line.
alt: Crates of used books at an outdoor stall, titles facing out. Inventory alerts should be as countable as those spines, and stay inside the stall until a person speaks to a customer.
caption: Titles facing out, countable, still inside the stall. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Who should receive a low-stock alert?
faqs.answer: A named person who can reorder or decide to sell out, not a crowded channel where everyone assumes someone else saw it. The alert can repeat slowly while the condition holds. Hourly pings teach the team to mute the one signal that mattered.

faqs.question: Should customers get a restock email automatically?
faqs.answer: They can join a list automatically. The send should wait until a person knows the goods are actually in and sellable. A quantity that flicks above zero and back is not a restock. Scarcity lines such as "only two left" need a real count a person will defend.

faqs.question: What is a bad zero in an inventory feed?
faqs.answer: A zero that means the sync failed, not that the shelf is empty. The workflow should tell those apart and wake someone about the failure. Selling against a broken feed, or stopping sales because of one, is the expensive version of this project.

markdown:
Inventory alert automation should tell the person who reorders that a number crossed a line they chose. It should not email customers a restock date, invent scarcity, or take payment for something you cannot ship. The count is a fact. The promise is a relationship.

Automate the handoff around stock that is about to run out. The machine may watch the quantity, compare it to a threshold, and draft an internal note. Keep a person on anything a customer will see, anything they might pay, and anything you cannot undo, such as a preorder or a sold-out state that hides the product. Measure minutes of counting and chasing against minutes spent on false alarms and retracted promises.

## The threshold is a decision, not a default

Pick the number with the person who knows lead time. A threshold copied from a template, "alert at 10," is meaningless if the supplier takes twelve weeks or if ten units is a normal Tuesday. Write the threshold next to the product, and write why: enough cover until the next making, or enough to finish the current orders and then stop.

Different products get different lines. A made-to-order chair is not the same problem as a jar you can reprint a label for. A digital file does not need a stock alert at all. If the workflow treats every SKU as a pile of identical units, turn it off for the ones that are made when ordered, and track those as capacity, which is a person's calendar, not a quantity in a bin.

Review the thresholds when you change a supplier or a season. An alert set in a quiet month will scream in a busy one, and the team will mute the channel. A muted alert is worse than no alert, because everyone believes someone else is watching.

## What the internal alert contains

The note to your own people can be automatic. It should be specific.

- The product name and the variant, not only a SKU if the SKU is obscure to the person who must act.
- The quantity on hand, the threshold, and the time of the count.
- Open orders already promised against that quantity, if you have them, so "twelve left" is not "twelve we can still sell."
- Who is supposed to reorder or to decide to let it sell out.

Send it to a named role. A channel called "ops" with twelve people is a place for the alert to die. One owner, and a second person if the first is away. The alert repeats on a slow cadence you choose, such as once a day while the condition holds, not every hour. Hourly repetition teaches people to ignore it, which means the automation saved no minutes and added noise.

Do not let the alert "recommend" an order quantity unless the recommendation is arithmetic you wrote: target stock minus on hand minus incoming. A model that suggests a clever buy will be wrong in a way that looks confident, and the invoice to the supplier is money. A person places the purchase. The draft can prefill the supplier, the variant, and the arithmetic so the order starts from facts.

If the count itself may be wrong, say so in the alert when the last sync failed. A zero that means "the feed broke" is not a stockout. The workflow should distinguish a failed read from a true zero, and it should wake someone about the failure. Selling against a broken feed, or stopping sales because of one, is the expensive version of this project.

## What customers are allowed to see

A customer-facing stock line is a claim. "Only two left" creates urgency, and it is a lie if you set the line for effect. Do not let a tool turn a threshold into scarcity copy. If you show a quantity, show a quantity a person is willing to defend, and accept that it must update when the number changes. Stale scarcity is how a shop looks dishonest.

"Sold out" and "back soon" are different sentences. Sold out means they cannot check out that variant. A person should confirm the first time you hide a buy button, because that is close to a payment decision: you are refusing the sale, or you are about to take money you cannot fulfill. After the rule is trusted, the page can follow the count. The first weeks belong to a person watching the page, not only the alert channel.

A restock email is a promise with a date hiding inside it, even when you omit the date. "We will email you when it returns" is acceptable only if you will. The signup can be automatic. The send waits until a person knows the goods are actually in and sellable. A draft can sit ready. Releasing it because the quantity flicked above zero for an hour, then flicking it back, is how you write to people and then fail them.

Do not take preorder payment inside the alert workflow. Preorder is a product decision: what you will make, by when, and what you will do if you cannot. That belongs in the shop's normal checkout, written by a person, with the terms visible. An alert that converts itself into a charge is the thing you cannot undo politely.

The [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) applies when the stock state is on the page. The W3C's four principles are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A sold-out state should be text, not only a greyed button or a color. A person using the page should understand whether they can buy. If you tell them the item will return, the sentence has to be one you can keep. Accessibility here is the same discipline as honesty: say the state in words.

## Minutes saved against minutes of repair

Time a week of the old way. Who counts, how they count, how often a surprise stockout means a customer email you did not expect? Include those emails. They are the cost of a late human count.

Time the new way. Minutes to read true alerts and place the reorder, plus minutes spent on false alarms, plus minutes spent retracting a customer promise. If false alarms dominate, the threshold or the feed is wrong. Fix that before you add more SKUs to the workflow. A noisy alert on twenty products will be ignored on the one product that mattered.

Count customer-facing mistakes for a month: restock notes for items that were not ready, scarcity lines that were not real, orders accepted that you could not ship. The target is zero. Internal alerts can be wrong once in a while if a person catches them before a customer hears. External mistakes mean you put the send back behind a person.

Do not score the project by how many alerts fired. A quiet week with correct stock is a good week. An exciting channel is not a result.

## Incoming stock and the pages that must match

When a reorder is placed, the workflow can track "incoming" as a separate number from "on hand." Do not add incoming to the quantity a customer can buy unless fulfillment can ship incoming goods. Many small brands cannot. The alert to the team may say both numbers. The product page should say only what they can have.

When goods arrive, a person confirms the count against the delivery, then the on-hand number updates, then any restock draft becomes eligible. Skip the confirmation and you will email customers about a shipment that was short or wrong. The five minutes at the door are part of the automation's success, not a step to delete.

Variants need their own thresholds. A shirt that is gone in one size is not gone in every size. An alert that says the product is out, and a page that then hides every size, creates a false stockout and a support thread. The handoff has to be as granular as the thing you sell.

If you make to order, replace the alert with a capacity note: how many you can start this month, owned by a person. The site can say the lead time they approved. It should not count down a fictional bin.

## When to mute, and when to stop

Mute a product when you intend to sell it out and not reorder. Otherwise the alert will nag you to undo a decision you already made. Record the mute next to the product so the next person does not "fix" it by turning the alert back on and emailing customers.

Stop the customer-facing parts the moment a feed is untrusted. Keep the internal failure alert. A week of "we are not sure of the count, a person is checking" is a respectable state. Automatic certainty during a broken sync is how you take orders you cannot see.

Write the owner, the threshold, and the rule for restock mail in one place the team can open. A stock workflow that lives only inside a tool's settings will be wrong the first time that person is away, and the customer will meet the wrongness as a promise.

The next handoff is the new client, not the next unit. [Automating onboarding checklist without losing the relationship](/blog/automating-onboarding-checklist-without-losing-the-relationship) follows this one, because week one is a list of access and files, and the wrong share or the wrong welcome is as hard to undo as a false restock note.
